explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Pilate asks Jesus straight out, "Are You the King of the Jews?" and Jesus replies, "You have said so…" (Mark 15:2) That is not a no. Jesus doesn't tell Pilate He isn't.

Right, friend. Pilate asks, "Are You the King of the Jews?" and Jesus answers, "You have said so…" (Mark 15:2) He never tells Pilate He isn't. Keep an ear out for how short that answer is, because Jesus doesn't say much to Pilate in this passage.

That's it, baker. The text says, "…to Pilate’s amazement, Jesus made no further reply." (Mark 15:5) Pilate had just pointed at a mountain of charges and asked for an answer, and he got silence. I think I'd be staring too.

Close, but the text doesn't say that. It says Jesus "…made no further reply." and that this was "…to Pilate’s amazement…" (Mark 15:5) Pilate is amazed, and that's the only reaction Mark gives us here.

Not here, baker. In this verse the text gives one reaction: "…to Pilate’s amazement, Jesus made no further reply." (Mark 15:5) Mark doesn't say Pilate was afraid. He was amazed that the man with all those charges against Him wouldn't say more.

Yes, baker. "…the crowd went up and began asking Pilate to keep his custom." (Mark 15:8) That custom was to release a prisoner of their choosing at the feast (Mark 15:6). The crowd is asking him to do what he always does. That's the ask.

Nope, the crowd isn't asking for that. Mark says they "…began asking Pilate to keep his custom." (Mark 15:8) That means releasing a prisoner for them at the feast (Mark 15:6). Nobody is asking him to cut the party short.

Not this time, baker. The crowd came to ask Pilate "…to keep his custom." (Mark 15:8) That custom was releasing a prisoner of their choosing at the feast (Mark 15:6). Nothing here says they asked to judge the case themselves.

You got it, baker. "…the chief priests stirred up the crowd to have him release Barabbas to them instead." (Mark 15:11) Barabbas was the man imprisoned with the rebels who had committed murder (Mark 15:7). The crowd got a push, and it came from the chief priests.

Good guess, but Mark doesn't mention any money. The text says the chief priests "…stirred up the crowd to have him release Barabbas to them instead." (Mark 15:11) Stirring up is the word the text uses for what they did.

Not quite, friend. Mark says the chief priests "…stirred up the crowd…" (Mark 15:11) It doesn't say they warned anybody. The text tells us what the chief priests did, and the goal was to have Barabbas released instead.

Yes, baker. "And they shouted back, 'Crucify Him!'" (Mark 15:13) Pilate had asked what to do with the One they call the King of the Jews. That's the crowd's answer. I think this is a heavy moment, so let's let it be heavy.

That's not what they shouted, baker. Pilate had floated the idea of releasing Jesus (Mark 15:9), but the crowd "shouted back, 'Crucify Him!'" (Mark 15:13) The answer to his question was the opposite of release.
Not this one, friend. Mark records the crowd's words exactly: "Crucify Him!" (Mark 15:13) They didn't ask for Jesus to be sent away. It's a hard line to read, and that's the line.

Not quite, baker. Pilate asks, "Why? What evil has He done?" and the crowd doesn't go quiet. Mark says, "they shouted all the louder, 'Crucify Him!'" (Mark 15:14) He asked for a reason and got more volume.

Right, baker. Pilate asks, "Why? What evil has He done?" and the crowd doesn't go quiet. Mark says, "they shouted all the louder, 'Crucify Him!'" (Mark 15:14). It's the same two words again. The crowd's answer just got louder.

That's right, baker. Mark says, "…wishing to satisfy the crowd, Pilate released Barabbas to them." (Mark 15:15) Barabbas was the man imprisoned with the rebels who had committed murder (Mark 15:7). The text gives us Pilate's reason, and it's the crowd.

Not this time, friend. Mark says, "…wishing to satisfy the crowd, Pilate released Barabbas to them." (Mark 15:15) The text gives that as his reason. Barabbas was the man imprisoned with the rebels who had committed murder (Mark 15:7).

Yes, baker. The soldiers "…twisted together a crown of thorns, and set it on His head." (Mark 15:17) They also dressed Him in a purple robe. I think this part of the passage is a hard one to read, so let's read it slowly.
Not here, baker. Mark says the soldiers "…twisted together a crown of thorns, and set it on His head." (Mark 15:17) There are no stars in this scene. These soldiers twisted thorns together.
No gold in this scene, friend. The soldiers "…twisted together a crown of thorns, and set it on His head." (Mark 15:17) They had put a purple robe on Him as well. The crown was made of thorns.

That's it, baker. "They began to salute Him: 'Hail, King of the Jews!'" (Mark 15:18) Pilate had used the title King of the Jews when he questioned Jesus (Mark 15:2). Here the soldiers use it in their salute, along with the robe and the crown.
Close, but the soldiers didn't say that. They saluted Him: "Hail, King of the Jews!" (Mark 15:18) Mark gives us their exact words. Son of David isn't one of them.
Not this time, baker. Mark records the soldiers saying, "Hail, King of the Jews!" (Mark 15:18) Nothing in this passage has them calling Jesus a prophet. They call Him a king.
Not quite, baker. Mark says, "After they had mocked Him, they removed the purple robe and put His own clothes back on Him." (Mark 15:20) The robe came off. His own clothes went back on.

Right, baker. Mark says, "After they had mocked Him, they removed the purple robe and put His own clothes back on Him." (Mark 15:20) So the robe doesn't stay on. His own clothes go back on Him. Then they led Him out to crucify Him.
